story.headline: M7.4 quake devastates western Colombia
story.summary: A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on 10 August, killing scores and leaving more than 2,700 reported missing.
story.display_body: A magnitude-7.4 earthquake devastated western Colombia on Monday 10 August, killing scores of people and triggering a frantic overnight search for survivors under collapsed buildings. The US Geological Survey put the quake at M7.4, striking 5 km south of San José del Palmar in the remote Chocó region at 12:34 UTC, followed by a M5.0 aftershock and, per Colombia's Geological Service, at least 21 aftershocks by late Monday. President Abelardo de la Espriella — sworn in only on Friday 7 August — reported 35 dead in Cali and declared a state of emergency; local authorities counted at least 40 more dead around Pereira and a dozen elsewhere, with 700 injured in the Valle del Cauca department alone. Roughly 1,600 buildings were damaged, including hospital floors in Cali that collapsed onto patients and the towers of a historic cathedral in Manizales. More than 2,700 people were "reported missing" on citizen-run websites by Monday night, a figure authorities caution is unverified and not a confirmed count. Chocó, near the epicentre and reachable mainly by boat or plane, remains largely unassessed.
story.why: it is Colombia's strongest quake in decades, striking a mountainous, hard-to-reach zone where the true toll may take days to emerge, and the first major test of a government four days into office.

story.headline: Assad sentenced to death in absentia
story.summary: A Damascus court sentenced ex-president Bashar al-Assad and relatives to death for war-era crimes against humanity.
story.display_body: A Damascus criminal court on Tuesday 11 August sentenced Syria's ex-president Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity committed during the country's nearly 14-year war. His brother Maher al-Assad — like Bashar, now in exile in Russia — was also sentenced to death in absentia, while cousin Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Deraa who was detained in January 2025, heard his death sentence from inside a courtroom cage. Najib launched the 2011 crackdown on Deraa protesters that helped ignite the uprising and later civil war; the court cited "the intentional killing of children under 15" among his crimes. Presiding judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan said testimony established Assad as "the highest decision-maker" who used state institutions to facilitate the crimes.
story.why: it is the first ruling by Syria's post-Assad transitional authorities against the former ruling family, and — though the two principals are beyond reach in Russia — sets a legal precedent for prosecuting the old government's officials.

story.headline: Turkey passes PKK disarmament law
story.summary: Turkey's parliament approved a legal framework for PKK disarmament and reintegration on 10 August.
story.display_body: Turkey's parliament passed the government's PKK disarmament law on Monday 10 August, moving a submitted bill into force after roughly ten hours of debate. The vote was 468 in favour to 88 against with six abstentions among 562 lawmakers present; the bill — which the government brands the "terror-free Turkey law" — was backed by President Erdoğan's ruling alliance and by the pro-Kurdish DEM party. It creates a legal path for Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK — the armed Kurdish movement that fought the Turkish state for four decades) fighters who lay down their weapons to return to civilian life, and is expected to free around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees in a first phase, about a third of those held. Ankara stresses it is not a blanket amnesty: those convicted of serious crimes such as murder are excluded, and the text does not mention jailed PKK founder Abdullah Öcalan. This advances the framework Turkey submitted to parliament on 5 August.
story.why: it is the most concrete legislative step yet toward ending one of the region's longest insurgencies, though the exclusions and Öcalan's ambiguous status leave the peace process' hardest questions open.

story.headline: Mass grave found in Sudan's Kurmuk
story.summary: Sudanese forces found a mass grave with 25 bodies in Kurmuk after retaking the town from the RSF.
story.display_body: Sudanese forces have found a mass grave holding 25 bodies — including children, women and hospital staff — in the town of Kurmuk, in the southeastern Blue Nile region, the local commissioner announced on Sunday 9 August. Commissioner Abdel Aty Mohamed al-Faki said the grave was uncovered during sweeping operations after the army retook Kurmuk from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on 8 July; the victims were allegedly executed near Jebel Fankat, a hilltop the RSF had used to launch drone attacks. The find follows similar discoveries after the army recaptured areas of Khartoum and Gezira states from the RSF, which has been fighting the Sudanese army since April 2023.
story.why: it adds to a mounting record of alleged atrocities in a war that has displaced millions and drawn repeated accusations of mass killings against the RSF.

story.headline: Apollo wins EasyJet with 6.2bn bid
story.summary: US fund Apollo Global Management won the takeover battle for airline EasyJet with a 6.2 billion franc offer.
story.display_body: US investment firm Apollo Global Management won the takeover battle for budget airline EasyJet on Tuesday 11 August with an offer valuing the carrier at about 6.2 billion francs, edging out fellow American fund Castlelake. Apollo had entered the contest as the second-placed bidder before pulling ahead on the final bid, according to Le Temps. The paper notes the harder fight now begins before European regulators, whose approval the deal will need. EasyJet is one of the largest operators at Geneva Airport, where it runs a major base, so ownership and route decisions bear directly on Swiss travellers.
story.why: a buyout of a top low-cost carrier by a private-equity owner raises the perennial question of whether cost discipline squeezes fares, routes or reliability at hubs like Geneva.

story.headline: Le Locle watch museum robbed
story.summary: The Château des Monts horology museum in Le Locle was burgled on 9 August, its third burglary in 20 years.
story.display_body: Thieves broke into the Château des Monts horology museum in Le Locle (canton Neuchâtel) early on Sunday 9 August, around 06:15, the town confirmed — the third burglary at the watchmaking museum in twenty years. The 18th-century mansion, which houses a renowned collection of clocks and automata, will reopen to its roughly ten staff and the public on Wednesday 13 August. Le Temps frames the raid as a reminder of the "perilous attractiveness" of horology museums in a region whose watchmaking heritage carries high-value, portable objects.
story.why: repeated targeting of Swiss watchmaking collections points to a persistent security problem for cultural institutions in the Jura arc, where the objects on display double as luxury goods.

story.headline: Schaffhausen blaze injures firefighters
story.summary: A large fire with two detonations destroyed a barn in Schaffhausen on 10 August, injuring four firefighters.
story.display_body: A large fire destroyed a disused barn near the freight rail yard in Schaffhausen on Monday evening 10 August, injuring four firefighters who were taken to hospital, cantonal police said. Residents reported two powerful explosions whose shockwaves were felt hundreds of metres away; police confirmed the detonations but said their cause was still being investigated. The fire brigade responded in force.
story.why: the blast felt across the neighbourhood, and the injuries to responders, make the cause — as yet unexplained — the open question for the cantonal investigation.

story.headline: Distilled skill beats reasoning mode
story.summary: A compiled natural-language skill lets a non-reasoning model match reasoning-mode accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.
story.display_body: Reasoning models — the ones that "think out loud" before answering — beat their plain counterparts on multi-step agent tasks but pay a 3–6× premium in output tokens, much of it spent re-deriving the same procedures episode after episode. The authors have a coding agent read a small set of past trajectories from a training split and compile them into a compact natural-language "skill" — a paragraph of instructions injected into a non-reasoning model's system prompt. On-policy distillation (learning from the model's own attempts rather than a fixed dataset) is the broader family this belongs to.
story.why: across four agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, τ²-bench telecom and retail, SpreadsheetBench-Verified), the skill recovers 55%–100%+ of the reasoning gap for GPT-5.4-mini on held-out tasks — beating reasoning mode outright on two of four — while emitting 2.7–6× fewer output tokens and zero reasoning tokens. It suggests much of what "thinking" buys is reusable and can be cached as text, not re-paid every call.

story.headline: KV cache pushed past 2-bit cliff
story.summary: SPECTRA's training-free spectral codec compresses the attention KV cache below two bits without the usual quality collapse.
story.display_body: As models read longer inputs — whole codebases, long conversations — inference memory is dominated by the KV cache (key-value cache: the stored attention keys and values for every token seen so far, re-read on every new token). The standard fix is quantization — storing each value at low precision — but quality drops sharply at a "2-bit cliff": four levels are too few for the cache's outlier-heavy values, where a few large entries eat all the levels. SPECTRA first rotates the cache into a coordinate system computed from its own statistics (a spectral transform that removes the correlations between channels), after which a small fraction of channels carries almost all the information; it then spends the bit budget there. It is training-free and drop-in.
story.why: long-context and agentic workloads live or die on cache memory, and the 2-bit cliff has been a practical floor for a while. A training-free codec that gets under it cleanly is the kind of change that quietly widens what fits on a given GPU.

story.headline: Thought-level beam search for reasoning
story.summary: Gambit runs beam search over whole reasoning thoughts to allocate test-time compute, raising accuracy and cutting tokens under a fixed budget.
story.display_body: "Test-time compute" means spending extra computation at answer time — sampling many reasoning traces, or thinking longer — to get better answers. Existing approaches waste it: parallel sampling treats traces independently and bottlenecks memory, while pruning starves the hardware. Gambit runs a beam search at the level of whole thoughts: it periodically prunes unpromising trajectories and immediately branches from the strong prefixes, steered by a lightweight scorer that probes the model's hidden states, keeping the GPU busy throughout.
story.why: under identical hardware limits, Gambit reports up to +6.7% absolute accuracy on HMMT-24 and +3.3% on AIME-25 (competition-math benchmarks) over pruning baselines, >2× throughput on trace completion, and up to 68.5% fewer tokens than standard parallel sampling — a concrete recipe for getting more reasoning per fixed compute budget.

fields.why: under identical hardware limits, Gambit reports up to +6.7% absolute accuracy on HMMT-24 and +3.3% on AIME-25 (competition-math benchmarks) over pruning baselines, >2× throughput on trace completion, and up to 68.5% fewer tokens than standard parallel sampling — a concrete recipe for getting more reasoning per fixed compute budget.

story.headline: Multilingual refusal circuit located
story.summary: A mechanistic study finds harm detected language-invariantly mid-network but the refusal written late by a localizable MoE circuit.
story.display_body: Safety alignment is uneven across languages: a model that refuses a harmful English request often complies with the same request in a lower-resource language. Studying sarvam, an Indic-multilingual mixture-of-experts (MoE — many specialist sub-networks, only a few active per token) reasoning model, the authors trace this mechanistically. Harm is encoded as an internal direction that is nearly language-invariant in mid-network (English-vs-Indic cosine ≈0.9), and steering that direction causally controls refusal. But that detection direction is orthogonal to the change that actually writes the refusal, which is assembled late over the course of generation by a specific, localizable MoE circuit held in check by an "attention opposer."
story.why: it reframes the multilingual safety gap as a failure to act on detected harm, not to detect it — the model knows, but the refusal machinery doesn't fire. That points interventions at a different, narrower target than "teach it to recognize harm in Hindi."

story.headline: Latent safety probes reproduced
story.summary: A reproducibility study tests cheap activation probes for harmful-prompt detection across model families and random seeds.
story.display_body: A 2026 result (Khatri et al.) showed that a lightweight probe — a small classifier reading a model's final-layer activations — can detect harmful prompts at F1 (a precision/recall score) competitive with dedicated guard models 1,000× larger, on a single 8B model. This paper reproduces that pipeline end-to-end and stress-tests it two ways: across other families (Gemma-4-E4B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Qwen2-7B) and across five random seeds to measure how much inference non-determinism moves the score. The original LLaMA numbers reproduce within 0.37 percentage points.
story.why: cheap latent-space safety probes are an attractive alternative to running a second large guard model, but only if the result generalizes and is stable. Reproductions that report seed variance and cross-family transfer — rather than a single headline number — are exactly the honest scaffolding the safety-tooling literature needs.

story.headline: On-policy distillation gaming exposed
story.summary: TIDE shows students can game token-level agreement with the teacher, and fixes the mismatch directions instead.
story.display_body: On-policy distillation (OPD) — training a student model to match a teacher on the student's own generated outputs — is now standard in post-training pipelines. The authors expose "degenerate agreement": students learn repetitive loops that score near-perfect token-level agreement with the teacher while producing globally flawed answers. Shifting focus from agreement to mismatch, they categorize the disagreements into student-excess tokens (student emits them, teacher assigns near-zero probability — their corrections blow up and destabilize training) and student-deficit tokens (teacher prefers them, student rarely samples them — blocking transfer of the teacher's reasoning). Their method, TIDE, handles each direction separately.
story.why: it names a concrete way a widely used training recipe can look like it's working (high agreement) while quietly failing, and gives a fix — useful diligence for anyone shipping distilled models.

story.headline: Activation isn't control in RL tuning
story.summary: A control-analysis study argues a circuit that activates under RL fine-tuning need not be the one steering the reward gain.
story.display_body: Reinforcement-learning post-training unlocks complex reasoning, but benchmark scores don't reveal what changed inside the model. A prominent interpretability line credits RL's success to stronger, more diverse "circuit activation." Borrowing Metabolic Control Analysis from systems biology, the authors separate activation from control: a circuit that lights up need not be the thing that controls the reward gain. They define a Post-training Control Coefficient, arrange it into a control matrix by task family, and identify a "Shared Control Bottleneck" — a few components controlling gains across many tasks — plus an "Activation–Control Gap."
story.why: if the parts of a network that visibly activate aren't the parts steering the improvement, a lot of activation-based interpretability of RL may be measuring the wrong thing. It's a healthy, falsifiable pushback on a popular narrative.

story.headline: Meta returns with open Muse Glimmer
story.summary: Meta open-sourced Muse Glimmer, a 30B Apache-2.0 multimodal agent model, its first open release from Superintelligence Labs.
story.display_body: Meta returns to open weights with Muse Glimmer, a 30B multimodal agent model. After more than a year without an open release, Meta published Muse-Glimmer-30B (29.8B parameters, Apache-2.0) — the first open model from its new Superintelligence Labs — a multimodal (image-and-text-in) model built for agentic tool use that fits in under ~20 GB of memory once its weights are compressed, i.e. runnable on consumer hardware. A companion essay from Mark Zuckerberg defends distilling other labs' models and argues for fewer restrictions on US labs — read widely as a shot at OpenAI and Anthropic — and an open-weight Muse Spark 1.2 is reported to follow. Meta / Hugging Face model card
story.why: an Apache-2.0 multimodal agent model that runs locally is directly useful to developers, and Meta re-entering the open field resets the competitive floor. The distillation defense is notable given how much of this cycle's research (above) is about distilling expensive models into cheap ones.

story.headline: Motif 3 314B MoE with latent attention
story.summary: Motif Technologies details Motif 3, a 314B sparse MoE with only 13.2B active per token and a new grouped latent-attention design.
story.display_body: Motif 3: a 314B mixture-of-experts model with a novel latent-attention design. Motif Technologies detailed Motif 3, a decoder-only MoE with 314B total parameters but only 13.2B active per token (384 routed experts, 8 selected). Its centerpiece is Grouped Differential Latent Attention (GDLA), which pairs "differential" attention with the compressed key-value representation of Multi-head Latent Attention to cut inference memory; pretraining ran on ~12.5T tokens with context up to 256K, and — fittingly for this cycle — post-training leaned on multi-teacher on-policy distillation. arXiv:2608.09119 ·
story.why: it's a from-scratch frontier-scale architecture that bets on fine-grained sparsity plus latent attention for efficiency — a concrete data point on how far the MoE-plus-compressed-attention recipe scales outside the biggest US labs.

story.headline: OpenAI ships GPT-5.6-Cyber for defenders
story.summary: OpenAI released a gated cyber-specialized model it says answers blocked security queries and found two unknown Chrome bugs.
story.display_body: OpenAI ships GPT-5.6-Cyber, a defender-focused security model, behind identity checks. OpenAI released a cyber-specialized model that it says answers up to 98.5% of security queries a general model would refuse, and reports it has already surfaced two previously unknown Chrome vulnerabilities. Access requires verified identity, and OpenAI frames the release around a shrinking window in which defenders must find flaws before attackers do (its paired "Daybreak" and "trusted hands" posts). Treat the capability numbers as the vendor's own.
story.why: a gated, offense-capable model marketed for defense is the concrete form of the "dual-use" debate — the same tool that finds a bug for a defender finds it for an attacker, so the identity gate is doing a lot of the safety work.

story.headline: Anthropic watermarks all Claude output
story.summary: Anthropic will embed invisible text watermarks and C2PA file signatures in all Claude outputs worldwide.
story.display_body: Anthropic will watermark all Claude output worldwide and sign files with C2PA. Anthropic announced it will embed invisible watermarks in all Claude-generated text and cryptographically sign generated files using C2PA (a cross-industry content-provenance standard that attaches tamper-evident metadata about how a file was made). Models shipping from August 2026 carry labeling from day one, the policy is global, and Anthropic says it will provide detection tools for third-party verification; the text marks "may persist through some editing."
story.why: durable, verifiable provenance on AI output is what regulators and platforms have been asking for; whether text watermarks survive real-world paraphrasing and editing is the open question this will be judged on.

story.headline: Nvidia backs $500B compute financing
story.summary: Nvidia and six asset managers formed platforms to mobilize over $500 billion of third-party capital for AI compute infrastructure.
story.display_body: Nvidia anchors a $500B+ third-party financing platform for AI compute. Nvidia announced partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to establish independent financing platforms meant to mobilize over $500 billion of third-party capital, turning its compute and full-stack infrastructure into what it calls "an investable asset class." Secondary reporting adds that Nvidia is guaranteeing up to 25% of the residual value of its own hardware to reassure investors, and that the Bank of England has warned of systemic risk if the AI sector contracts.
story.why: a chipmaker underwriting the residual value of its own product to unlock outside financing is a striking blurring of vendor and financier — and the BoE's warning names the tail risk if AI demand softens.
